title: The winter solstice
hook: the longest night, and the light returns from here

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Saturnalia, when masters served and Seneca kept a sober head. Your line was roles reversed. Who did you give something to? Day six hundred seventy-three.

Four-thirty in the afternoon and it's already dark. You leave work in the dark; you might have arrived in it too. In the far north, the sun barely clears the horizon, or doesn't rise at all. And yet, all around the world, this darkest stretch of the year is full of lights. Strings of them on houses. Candles in windows. In Iran, families stay up through Yalda, the longest night, eating pomegranates and reading poetry. Many traditions keep their own festivals of light around now, each with its own meaning. Today on the porch: the winter solstice.
screen: `DARK AT FOUR-THIRTY.` → `CANDLES IN WINDOWS.` → `THE LONGEST NIGHT.`

segments.voice: First, the turn at the bottom. Back at the summer solstice, we saw that the peak of the light was also the start of its going. Now it's the mirror: the longest night is the moment the light starts coming back. Tomorrow will be a little longer than today. Nobody will notice, at first. Second, Seneca on the seasons. In one of his late letters, he tells Lucilius that the world itself runs on change. Winter brings the cold, and we have to shiver. Summer brings the heat, and we have to sweat. We can't change that order, he says, but we can take on a great spirit, worthy of a good person, and bear what comes bravely, in agreement with nature. The dark isn't a punishment. It's part of the turning. Third, a Stoic and his lamp. Epictetus tells his students that he once had an iron lamp by his household gods, and a thief stole it. His response: tomorrow, I'll buy a clay one. The thief lost more than he did, Epictetus says, because he became a thief for the price of a lamp. A light, for Epictetus, is something you can always light again. Fourth, why a candle. A candle in the dark doesn't argue with the night. It doesn't make it day. It just makes a small circle where you can see a face, a page, your own hands. That's often what getting through a hard season looks like: not ending the dark, but keeping one small light going until the days lengthen on their own.
screen: `THE LONGEST NIGHT IS ALSO THE TURN.` · `WINTER BRINGS COLD: WE SHIVER.` · `EPICTETUS'S STOLEN LAMP.` · `A SMALL CIRCLE OF LIGHT.` · then, large: `THE LIGHT RETURNS.`

segments.voice: If you can, light a candle, safely, somewhere you can watch it. If not, turn on one small lamp and turn the others off. Look at the flame or the glow. Notice how far the light reaches, and where the dark begins. Don't try to push the dark away. Let the small light be enough. Think of one person who's in a dark season right now. Hold them in mind in this small circle of light. The bell holds the time.
The winter solstice: the longest night of the year, and the turning point after which the light returns, little by little. Today's word.
Your line: the light returns. Light one small light tonight, a candle or a lamp, and if someone you love is in the dark, send them a few words. Day six hundred seventy-three.

howItsDone: Many traditions hold festivals of light around the winter solstice, each with its own meaning; some people mark the longest night simply by lighting a candle and keeping company.

what a scholar hears: Letters 107 tells Lucilius that winter brings cold and we must shiver, and that a great spirit accepts nature's order; Discourses 1.18 and 1.29 tell the story of the stolen iron lamp.

notes: Letters 107 paraphrased (winter brings cold, we must shiver; summer heat, we must swelter; we cannot change this order, but can take on a great soul and endure in harmony with nature). Confirm section numbers.
Epictetus's iron lamp stolen, 'tomorrow you will find an earthenware one'; the thief became a thief for a lamp: Discourses 1.18.15 and 1.29.21. Confirm.
Yalda (Shab-e Yalda) customs: staying up, pomegranates, reading Hafez. Confirm general description.
Festivals of light mentioned generally without naming or comparing them.
